images.caption: Office building (LVM 7 and 6) of the LVM Insurance in Münster, North Rhine-Westphalia, GermanyThe origins of today’s LVM campus date back to 1967, when the company moved into its premises on Kolde-Ring at the corner of Weseler Straße. The campus’s seven insurance buildings are located south of Münster city center. The northern part of Von-Stauffenberg-Straße runs through the campus, while Sperlichstraße forms its southern boundary. The LVM buildings were constructed between 1965 and 2014. The insurance company’s three high-rise buildings in particular are part of Münster’s skyline. The ground-level sculptures “Body and Soul” (Duk-Kyu Ryang, 2015) and “Two Horses for Münster” (Stephan Huber, 2002) are central visual elements of the site design. The 63-meter-high office tower LVM 5, known as “Crystal”, is a particularly striking building due to its design, while the 80-meter-high building LVM 3, known as “Tower”, is one of the tallest buildings in Münster.

images.caption: Prinzipalmarkt and St. Lamberti Church, Münster, North Rhine-Westphalia, GermanyPrinzipalmarkt is a street in Münster’s old town. The name means “main market”, in contrast to the nearby streets Roggenmarkt and Fischmarkt. With its layout and buildings, Prinzipalmarkt documents the historical and architectural development of Münster’s economic and political center. Its development as a bourgeois market street on the edge of the cathedral precinct and on the eastern border of the cathedral began in the 12th century. A closed development probably existed around 1280. At the turn of the 13th to 14th century, the arcade that characterizes the Prinzipalmarkt was built. It was not until the beginning of the 17th century that the name Prinzipalmarkt came into use. During World War II, most of the buildings on Prinzipalmarkt were completely destroyed, some down to their cellars and ground floors. Thanks to reconstruction work carried out between 1947 and 1958, Prinzipalmarkt was able to retain its character as an ensemble in the form of a historic market square. Compared to its pre-war state, many buildings were significantly altered, but the original impression remained intact.

images.caption: Open air museum Mühlenhof, Münster, North Rhine-Westphalia, GermanyThe Mühlenhof Open-Air Museum was founded in 1961 with the aim of preserving historic buildings and craftsmanship from the region. In 1963, the museum officially opened its doors to visitors, who have since had the opportunity to experience rural life of past centuries up close. Over time, the museum has been continuously expanded, with additional buildings illustrating different aspects of rural life and craftsmanship. In the 1980s, a mill complex was added to the museum, highlighting the Mühlenhof (mill farm) that gave it its name.
